q: A solution is a homogeneous (uniform) mixture of two or more substances.
e: In a solution, the solute is uniformly distributed throughout the solvent.

q: In a sugar-water mixture, sugar is the solvent and water is the solute.
e: Sugar is the solute, and water is the solvent.

q: Ethanol, acetic acid and sulphuric acid are soluble in water.
e: These liquids can mix with water in all proportions, making them miscible liquids.

q: Petrol and oils are soluble in water.
e: Petrol and oils are insoluble in water and are considered immiscible liquids.

q: Dry air is a familiar example of a gaseous solution.
e: Solutions may be gaseous, solid, or liquid in nature, and dry air is a gaseous solution.

q: Brass (copper and zinc) is an example of a liquid solution.
e: Brass is an example of a solid solution.

q: Solutions having water as the solvent are referred to as aqueous solutions.
e: Many reactions, including those vital for life processes, occur in aqueous solutions.

q: An unsaturated solution forms when no more solute can be dissolved in the given amount of solvent at that temperature.
e: A saturated solution forms when no more solute can be dissolved; an unsaturated solution can still dissolve more solute.

q: The amount (in grams) of the solute in 100 g of water to give a saturated solution at that experimental temperature is known as the solubility of that solute.
e: This is the standard definition of solubility provided in the textbook.

q: If the solution contains more solute than it should have at room temperature, it is a supersaturated solution.
e: A supersaturated solution retains more solute than that required to saturate the solution at room temperature.

q: When the temperature of the solution is increased, the solubility of the solute generally decreases.
e: When the temperature of the solution is increased, the solubility of the solute generally increases.

q: The solubility of all gases decreases when temperature of the solution is increased.
e: This is an exception to the general rule; gases, as well as some solids like calcium hydroxide, decrease in solubility with increased temperature.

q: Calcium hydroxide and calcium sulphate are exceptions whose solubility increases when temperature of the solution is increased.
e: The solubility of calcium hydroxide and calcium sulphate decreases when the temperature of the solution is increased.

q: When a saturated solution at a higher temperature is cooled, the solubility decreases.
e: As solubility decreases upon cooling, the excess solute will come out as a solid.

q: The excess solute will come out as a gas when a saturated solution at a higher temperature is cooled.
e: The excess solute will come out as a solid, not a gas, when the solution is cooled.

q: Some solids such as sand, charcoal and chalk are soluble in water.
e: Solids such as sand, charcoal and chalk are insoluble in water.

q: Some liquids can mix with one another in all proportions and are called miscible liquids.
e: This contrasts with immiscible liquids, which do not mix.

q: Carbonated water contains carbon dioxide gas molecules existing between molecules of water.
e: This is an example of a liquid solution containing a gaseous solute.

q: Blood and saliva are familiar solutions of biological importance.
e: These are examples of aqueous solutions vital for life processes.

q: More gas is released from a cold can of soda than from a warm one.
e: More gas is released from the warm pop than from the cold pop because gas solubility decreases as temperature increases.
